claim: Adult Drosophila Malpighian tubules have low rates of cell turnover.
source: Adult Drosophila Malpighian tubules have low rates of cell turnover but are vulnerable to damage caused by stones, like their mammalian counterparts, kidneys.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of the tissue under study.

claim: Drosophila Malpighian tubules are vulnerable to damage caused by stones.
source: Adult Drosophila Malpighian tubules have low rates of cell turnover but are vulnerable to damage caused by stones, like their mammalian counterparts, kidneys.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing stone formation and damage in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila renal stem cells (RSCs) are located in the ureter and lower tubules.
source: We show that Drosophilarenal stem cells (RSCs) in the ureter and lower tubules comprise a unique, unipotent regenerative compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data throughout the manuscript showing RSC localization.

claim: RSCs comprise a unique, unipotent regenerative compartment.
source: We show that Drosophilarenal stem cells (RSCs) in the ureter and lower tubules comprise a unique, unipotent regenerative compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lineage tracing and MARCM experiments showing RSCs only produce principal cells.

claim: RSCs respond only to loss of nearby principal cells (PCs).
source: RSCs respond only to loss of nearby principal cells (PCs), cells critical for maintaining ionic balance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by surgical injury experiments and cell ablation studies showing RSCs only respond to local PC loss.

claim: Principal cells are critical for maintaining ionic balance.
source: RSCs respond only to loss of nearby principal cells (PCs), cells critical for maintaining ionic balance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is consistent with established knowledge about principal cell function in Malpighian tubules.

claim: Large polyploid PCs are outnumbered by RSCs.
source: Large polyploid PCs are outnumbered by RSCs, which replace each lost cell with multiple PCs of lower ploidy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification data in Figure 1E showing RSCs comprise 66% of cells in the stem cell zone.

claim: RSCs replace each lost PC with multiple PCs of lower ploidy.
source: Large polyploid PCs are outnumbered by RSCs, which replace each lost cell with multiple PCs of lower ploidy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by nuclear volume measurements and regeneration experiments showing replacement PCs are smaller and lower ploidy.

claim: RSCs do not replenish principal cells or stellate cells in the upper tubules.
source: Notably, RSCs do not replenish principal cells or stellate cells in the upper tubules.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell ablation experiments and lineage tracing showing no replacement of upper tubule cells.

claim: RSCs generate daughters by asymmetric Notch signaling.
source: RSCs generate daughters by asymmetric Notch signaling, yet RSCs remain quiescent (cell cycle-arrested) without damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Notch reporter experiments, RNAi knockdown, and MARCM clone analysis.

claim: RSCs remain quiescent (cell cycle-arrested) without damage.
source: RSCs generate daughters by asymmetric Notch signaling, yet RSCs remain quiescent (cell cycle-arrested) without damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EdU incorporation assays, FUCCI analysis, and lack of mitotic markers under normal conditions.

claim: The capacity for RSC-mediated repair extends the lifespan of flies carrying kidney stones.
source: Nevertheless, the capacity for RSC-mediated repair extends the lifespan of flies carrying kidney stones.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lifespan experiments comparing control and RSC-depleted flies on allopurinol.

claim: Abundant, RSC-like stem cells may exist in other tissues with low rates of turnover where they may have been mistaken for differentiated tissue cells.
source: We propose that abundant, RSC-like stem cells exist in other tissues with low rates of turnover where they may have been mistaken for differentiated tissue cells.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings about RSCs in Drosophila Malpighian tubules.

claim: Highly active midgut intestinal stem cells (ISCs) produce regionally distinctive enterocytes and enteroendocrine cells throughout the midgut via asymmetric Notch signaling.
source: Highly active midgut intestinal stem cells (ISCs) produce regionally distinctive enterocytes and enteroendocrine cells throughout the midgut via asymmetric Notch signaling (Filshie et al., 1971; McNulty et al., 2001; Dubreuil, 2004; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007; Veenstra et al., 2008; Mehta et al., 2009; Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009; Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: ISCs respond to the demands of diet under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, ISCs respond to the demands of diet (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011; Obniski et al., 2018), differences in spatial location (Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), mechanical forces (He et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), the microbiota (Buchon et al., 2009a; Buchon et al., 2009b) and age (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008), all of which can influence the rate of cell turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ISCs respond to differences in spatial location under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, ISCs respond to the demands of diet (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011; Obniski et al., 2018), differences in spatial location (Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), mechanical forces (He et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), the microbiota (Buchon et al., 2009a; Buchon et al., 2009b) and age (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008), all of which can influence the rate of cell turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ISCs respond to mechanical forces under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, ISCs respond to the demands of diet (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011; Obniski et al., 2018), differences in spatial location (Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), mechanical forces (He et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), the microbiota (Buchon et al., 2009a; Buchon et al., 2009b) and age (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008), all of which can influence the rate of cell turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ISCs respond to the microbiota under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, ISCs respond to the demands of diet (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011; Obniski et al., 2018), differences in spatial location (Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), mechanical forces (He et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), the microbiota (Buchon et al., 2009a; Buchon et al., 2009b) and age (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008), all of which can influence the rate of cell turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ISCs respond to age under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, ISCs respond to the demands of diet (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011; Obniski et al., 2018), differences in spatial location (Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), mechanical forces (He et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), the microbiota (Buchon et al., 2009a; Buchon et al., 2009b) and age (Biteau et al., 2008; Choi et al., 2008), all of which can influence the rate of cell turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hindgut lacks specialized stem cells.
source: The hindgut lacks specialized stem cells and following damage is maintained primarily by induced polyploidization of post-mitotic epithelial cells (Fox and Spradling, 2009; Losick et al., 2013; Sawyer et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Following damage, the hindgut is maintained primarily by induced polyploidization of post-mitotic epithelial cells.
source: The hindgut lacks specialized stem cells and following damage is maintained primarily by induced polyploidization of post-mitotic epithelial cells (Fox and Spradling, 2009; Losick et al., 2013; Sawyer et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Adult Drosophila Malpighian tubules comprise the fastest known fluid-transporting epithelium.
source: The adult Drosophila excretory organ, the Malpighian tubules (MTs), comprise the fastest known fluid-transporting epithelium (Maddrell, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: MTs consist of initial, transitional, main and lower segments.
source: MTs represent an anatomically simple adjunct of the digestive system consisting of initial, transitional, main and lower segments (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The four Malpighian tubules branch from two common ureters that drain into the gut at the midgut/hindgut junction.
source: The four Malpighian tubules branch from two common ureters that drain into the gut at the midgut/hindgut junction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an anatomical description.

claim: The main segment of Malpighian tubules is responsible for fluid secretion.
source: It is commonly believed that the main segment of Malpighian tubules is responsible for fluid secretion, whereas the ureter and lower tubules are reabsorptive (Dow et al., 1994; O'Donnell and Maddrell, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ureter and lower tubules are reabsorptive.
source: It is commonly believed that the main segment of Malpighian tubules is responsible for fluid secretion, whereas the ureter and lower tubules are reabsorptive (Dow et al., 1994; O'Donnell and Maddrell, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The main segment of Malpighian tubules contains only two differentiated cell types, principal cells (PC) and stellate cells.
source: The main segment of Malpighian tubules contains only two differentiated cell types, principal cells (PC) and stellate cells, which are responsible for regulating ion balance and fluid secretion (reviewed in Gautam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Principal cells and stellate cells are responsible for regulating ion balance and fluid secretion.
source: The main segment of Malpighian tubules contains only two differentiated cell types, principal cells (PC) and stellate cells, which are responsible for regulating ion balance and fluid secretion (reviewed in Gautam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a review.

claim: MTs contain a distinct population of renal stem cells (RSCs) that express escargot (esg).
source: MTs contain a distinct population of renal stem cells (RSCs) that express escargot (esg) (Singh et al., 2007) and arise from the same pool of adult midgut progenitors that generate posterior midgut ISCs (Takashima et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RSCs arise from the same pool of adult midgut progenitors that generate posterior midgut ISCs.
source: MTs contain a distinct population of renal stem cells (RSCs) that express escargot (esg) (Singh et al., 2007) and arise from the same pool of adult midgut progenitors that generate posterior midgut ISCs (Takashima et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RSCs are located in the lower ureter, which develops from adult midgut progenitors.
source: RSCs are located both in the lower ureter, which develops from adult midgut progenitors, and in the upper ureter and lower segment of the Malpighian tubule (MT), which derive from the surviving larval ureter and larval MT (Takashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RSCs are located in the upper ureter and lower segment of the Malpighian tubule (MT), which derive from the surviving larval ureter and larval MT.
source: RSCs are located both in the lower ureter, which develops from adult midgut progenitors, and in the upper ureter and lower segment of the Malpighian tubule (MT), which derive from the surviving larval ureter and larval MT (Takashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RSCs were proposed to divide actively to produce daughter renoblasts (RBs) which migrate and endoreduplicate to replenish the two main MT cell types- principal cells (PCs) and stellate cells (SCs) located throughout the MT.
source: RSCs were proposed to divide actively to produce daughter renoblasts (RBs) which migrate and endoreduplicate to replenish the two main MT cell types- principal cells (PCs) and stellate cells (SCs) located throughout the MT (Singh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a prior proposal, which is later contradicted by the current study's findings.

claim: Follow-up studies demonstrated that RSCs are not active and divide slowly.
source: However, follow-up studies demonstrated that RSCs are not active and divide slowly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of prior work that contradicts earlier claims.

claim: Notch signaling and EGFR/MAPK signaling pathways regulate the differentiation and proliferation of RSCs, respectively.
source: Notch signaling and EGFR/MAPK signaling pathways regulate the differentiation and proliferation of RSCs, respectively (Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Two populations of principal cells are distinguishable based on size and ploidy: small PCs (4–16C) are found in the lower ureter, and large PCs (32–128C) reside in the upper ureter and Malpighian tubules.
source: Interestingly, two populations of principal cells are easily distinguishable based on size and ploidy: small PCs (4–16C) are found in the lower ureter, and large PCs (32–128C) reside in the upper ureter and Malpighian tubules (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging and nuclear volume measurements in Figure 1C and F.

claim: Both small PCs and large PCs express the homeobox protein Cut at high levels.
source: Both small PCs and large PCs express the homeobox protein Cut at high levels (Figure 1C1 and C2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining in Figure 1C1 and C2.

claim: esg-positive diploid cells are present only in the ureter and lower tubule (the stem cell zone (SCZ)).
source: We confirmed that esg-positive diploid cells are present only in the ureter and lower tubule (which we term 'the stem cell zone (SCZ)') using a Gal4 enhancer trap of esg to drive the expression of UAS-RFP (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 1C.

claim: The esg+ progenitor cells make up about 66% of cells in the SCZ.
source: Intriguingly, the esg+ progenitor cells make up about 66% of cells in the SCZ, more than the sum of small and large PCs (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1E.

claim: A low expression level of Cut is detected in esg+ stem cells.
source: We also detected a low expression level of Cut in esg+ stem cells (Figure 1C2 and D), consistent with a recent study (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining in Figure 1C2 and D, and a citation to prior work.

claim: The esg+ cell population slowly declines in number during adulthood.
source: We found that the esg+ cell population slowly declines in number during adulthood (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification in Figure 1G.

claim: 710 cells were sequenced and retained after quality control in the scRNA-seq experiment.
source: 710 cells were sequenced and retained after quality control.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a description of the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: The median genes that were recovered per cell is 1611 in the scRNA-seq experiment.
source: The median genes that were recovered per cell is 1611.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a description of the scRNA-seq experiment.

claim: Four major and one minor cell clusters were resolved in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: We used Seurat (Stuart et al., 2019) to do cell cluster assignment and four major and one minor cell clusters were resolved as shown in the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plot (McInnes et al., 1802; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the UMAP plot in Figure 2A.

claim: The four major cell groups correspond to RSCs (group 1) and three principal cell subtypes (group 2–4) based on expression of known markers.
source: The four major cell groups correspond to RSCs (group 1) and three principal cell subtypes (group 2–4) based on expression of known markers (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by marker gene expression in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The presence of a small population of Drip+ cells (group 5) is most likely due to contamination of stellate cells during dissection.
source: The presence of a small population of Drip+ cells (group 5) is most likely due to contamination of stellate cells during dissection since stellate cells in vivo are only found in the upper tubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on the known localization of stellate cells.

claim: RSCs were assigned to group 1 cells based on the enriched expression of esg.
source: RSCs were assigned to group 1 cells based on the enriched expression of esg.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a description of the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Group 1 cells expressed many genes such as Delta, Notch, and Sox21a that are important for ISC regulation.
source: Further analysis revealed that group 1 cells expressed many genes such as Delta, Notch, and Sox21a that are important for ISC regulation, and antibodies specific for Dl and Notch labeled RSCs (Figure 2D, E and G), consistent with the previous studies (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by scRNA-seq data and immunostaining in Figure 2D, E and G, and a citation to prior work.

claim: Antibodies specific for Dl and Notch labeled RSCs.
source: Further analysis revealed that group 1 cells expressed many genes such as Delta, Notch, and Sox21a that are important for ISC regulation, and antibodies specific for Dl and Notch labeled RSCs (Figure 2D, E and G), consistent with the previous studies (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunostaining in Figure 2D, E and G.

claim: Both Dl and Notch are present in esg+ RSCs, but Notch signaling activity was barely detectable in the adult Malpighian tubules.
source: Although both Dl and Notch are present in esg+ RSCs, Notch signaling activity was barely detectable in the adult Malpighian tubules, but readily detectable in midgut (Figure 2F), using a Notch signaling reporter construct expressing GFP under a Notch response element (NRE-GFP) (Saj et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by NRE-GFP reporter imaging in Figure 2F.

claim: RSCs were strikingly similar to ISCs in transcription factor expression.
source: By comparing transcription factor expression in group 1 RSCs with published data for ISCs to gain potential insight into cell identity (Dutta et al., 2015), we found that RSCs were strikingly similar to ISCs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and based on comparison with published ISC data.

claim: Relatively highly expressed TFs in RSCs were esg, Sox21a, E(spl)malpha-BFM, E(spl)mbeta-HLH, E(spl)m3-HLH, Sox100B, bun, zfh2, fkh, peb, Myc, Eip93F, Pdp1, Eip75B, and CrebA.
source: Relatively highly expressed TFs in RSCs were esg, Sox21a, E(spl)malpha-BFM, E(spl)mbeta-HLH, E(spl)m3-HLH, Sox100B, bun, zfh2, fkh, peb, Myc, Eip93F, Pdp1, Eip75B, and CrebA.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: All of the highly expressed TFs in RSCs are also expressed in ISCs.
source: All of these genes are also expressed in ISCs.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison with published ISC data.

claim: The chromatin decondensation factor 31 (Df31) is highly enriched in RSCs.
source: The chromatin decondensation factor 31 (Df31), which is associated with the establishment of open chromatin (Schubert et al., 2012), is highly enriched in RSCs (Figure 2H) and is also strongly expressed in ISCs (Dutta et al., 2015) (FlyGut-seq, http://flygutseq.buchonlab.com/).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 2H and citations to prior work.

claim: Df31 is also strongly expressed in ISCs.
source: The chromatin decondensation factor 31 (Df31), which is associated with the establishment of open chromatin (Schubert et al., 2012), is highly enriched in RSCs (Figure 2H) and is also strongly expressed in ISCs (Dutta et al., 2015) (FlyGut-seq, http://flygutseq.buchonlab.com/).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The principal cells (PC1-PC3) were assigned to clusters 2–4 based on the high expression of known principal cell marker genes including ct, Alp4, Uro and salt.
source: The principal cells (PC1-PC3) were assigned to clusters 2–4 based on the high expression of known principal cell marker genes including ct, Alp4, Uro and salt (Wallrath et al., 1990; Sözen et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2004; Stergiopoulos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by scRNA-seq data and citations to prior work.

claim: PCs expressed Ndae1, NaPi-T, Eglp2, Vha100-2, Irk2, Irk3 and ZnT35C, genes involved in ion transport.
source: PCs also expressed Ndae1, NaPi-T, Eglp2, Vha100-2, Irk2, Irk3 and ZnT35C, genes involved in ion transport.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The gene caudal (cad), which encodes a homeobox domain transcription factor essential for normal hindgut formation, was expressed in the PC1-PC3 cells.
source: The gene caudal (cad), which encodes a homeobox domain transcription factor essential for normal hindgut formation (Lh and Lengyel, 1998), was also expressed in the PC1-PC3 cells (Figure 2C and I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by scRNA-seq data in Figure 2C and imaging in Figure 2I, and a citation to prior work.

claim: A Gal4 enhancer trap line derived from the caudal (cad) gene specifically labeled principal cells in the ureter and the lower tubules.
source: As further validation, a Gal4 enhancer trap line derived from the caudal (cad) gene specifically labeled principal cells in the ureter and the lower tubules (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 2I.

claim: PC1 cells correspond to the principal cells in the distal lower tubules and proximal main segments.
source: The relatively lower expression of Alp4 and cad in PC1 cells suggested they are the principal cells in the distal lower tubules and proximal main segments, whose principal cells highly express Uro and salt (Wallrath et al., 1990; Stergiopoulos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on differential gene expression and citations to prior work.

claim: PC3 cells correspond to the small principal cells in the lower ureter.
source: The differential expression of Pvr between PC2 and PC3 cells enabled us to tell them apart (Figure 2C). A Pvr-GFP reporter construct was highly expressed in the principal cells of the lower ureter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). Thus PC3 cells correspond to the small principal cells in the lower ureter, whereas PC2 cells correspond to the large principal cells in the upper ureter and proximal lower tubules.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on differential gene expression and Pvr-GFP reporter imaging.

claim: PC2 cells correspond to the large principal cells in the upper ureter and proximal lower tubules.
source: The differential expression of Pvr between PC2 and PC3 cells enabled us to tell them apart (Figure 2C). A Pvr-GFP reporter construct was highly expressed in the principal cells of the lower ureter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). Thus PC3 cells correspond to the small principal cells in the lower ureter, whereas PC2 cells correspond to the large principal cells in the upper ureter and proximal lower tubules.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on differential gene expression and Pvr-GFP reporter imaging.

claim: Forced expression of UAS-hid, UAS-rpr for 7 days at 29°C with c507-Gal4ts led to nearly complete ablation of preexisting large PCs in the SCZ.
source: Forced expression of UAS-hid, UAS-rpr for 7 days at 29°C with c507-Gal4, tub-Gal80ts (referred to as c507-Gal4ts), which is a Gal4 enhancer trap line of Alp4 and specifically marks PCs in the SCZ (Yang et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), led to nearly complete ablation of preexisting large PCs in the SCZ.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a description of the PC ablation experiment.

claim: The regenerating SCZ was infiltrated with supernumerary small cells after PC ablation.
source: The regenerating SCZ was infiltrated with supernumerary small cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3A and B.

claim: After 21 days of recovery at 18°C, most small cells were gone and cells that were present appeared to be new PCs with high expression levels of Cut.
source: However, after 21 days of recovery at 18°C, most small cells were gone and cells that were present appeared to be new PCs with high expression levels of Cut (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The replacement cells did not express tsh, indicating they do not adopt stellate cell fate.
source: The replacement cells did not express the tsh as revealed by the lacZ enhancer trap line (tsh04319) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E), indicating they do not adopt stellate cell fate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: The replacement PCs have significantly smaller nuclei compared to preexisting PCs in the lower tubules.
source: Notably, the replacement PCs have significantly smaller nuclei compared to preexisting PCs in the lower tubules (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by nuclear volume quantification in Figure 3D.

claim: The replacement PCs resemble preexisting PCs in their transcriptomes.
source: In spite of distinct cell size, the replacement PCs resemble preexisting PCs in their transcriptomes as revealed by integrated analysis of scRNA-seq data across the wild type and regenerated tissues (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by integrated scRNA-seq analysis in Figure 3E.

claim: Surgical injury in the lower tubule promoted EdU incorporation into esg >RFP+ RSCs near the surgical site.
source: Surgical injury in the lower tubule promoted EdU incorporation into esg >RFP+ RSCs near the surgical site.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3G.

claim: Surgical injury in the upper tubule 5 PCs away from the SCZ slightly increased EdU incorporation in the RSCs at the most distal SCZ.
source: Surgical injury in the upper tubule 5 PCs away from the SCZ slightly increased EdU incorporation in the RSCs at the most distal SCZ.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3H.

claim: Surgical injury in the upper tubule 10 PCs away from the SCZ did not increase EdU incorporation in the RSCs.
source: Surgical injury in the upper tubule 10 PCs away from the SCZ did not increase EdU incorporation in the RSCs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging in Figure 3I.

claim: RSCs sense damage through short range signals extending less than ten cells away along the tubule.
source: This suggests that RSCs sense damage through short range signals extending less than ten cells away along the tubule.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on the surgical injury experiments.

claim: Cutting a tubule within the SCZ revealed a substantial increase in the number of RSC daughters near the surgical site.
source: Cutting a tubule within the SCZ and activating lineage tracing by temperature shift revealed a substantial increase in the number of RSC daughters (i.e. marked esg-) cells near the surgical site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and F', 1H), indicating that local RSCs were induced to generate esg- daughters by surgical injury in the SCZ.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by lineage tracing imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and F', 1H.

claim: Truncating the tubule within the main segment about 10 PCs away from the SCZ did not elicit any production of lineage-marked esg-cells in the SCZ up to 21 days post surgery.
source: In contrast, truncating the tubule within the main segment about 10 PCs away from the SCZ did not elicit any production of lineage-marked esg-cells in the SCZ up to 21 days post surgery (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and G',1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by lineage tracing imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and G',1H.

claim: Reporters for JNK, Jak/Stat, MAPK and Yki pathways were induced upon surgical injury.
source: Reporters for four of these pathways, JNK, Jak/Stat, MAPK and Yki pathways were induced upon surgical injury (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by reporter imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The JNK pathway was induced as early as 12–24 hr after injury in cells at the surgical site.
source: Interestingly, the JNK pathway was induced as early as 12–24 hr after injury in cells at the surgical site as revealed by the expression of UAS-GFP driven by pucE69-Gal4 (Adachi-Yamada, 2002), regardless of whether the surgical site was within the SCZ or in the distal upper tubules (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by reporter imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Upregulation of Jak/Stat and EGFR pathway reporters took place in RSCs close to the surgical site, which was only within the SCZ or in the proximal upper tubules.
source: However, upregulation of Jak/Stat and EGFR pathway reporters took place in RSCs close to the surgical site, which was only within the SCZ or in the proximal upper tubules, as assayed by the expression of 10XStat92E-GFP (Bach et al., 2007) and dpERK (Gabay et al., 1997), respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by reporter imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Diap1-lacZ was induced in cells near the surgical site within the SCZ, suggesting the Yki signaling was activated.
source: Diap1-lacZ, which is widely used as reporter of Yki activity (Huang et al., 2005), was also induced in cells near the surgical site within the SCZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D), suggesting the Yki signaling was activated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by reporter imaging in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: JNK pathway activation can induce the expression of Drosophila Jak/Stat pathway ligands (Upd1, Upd2 and Upd3), which in turn transduce Jak/Stat signaling in neighboring cells.
source: JNK pathway activation can induce the expression of Drosophila Jak/Stat pathway ligands (Upd1, Upd2 and Upd3), which in turn transduce Jak/Stat signaling in neighboring cells (Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RSCs are activated by damage-induced JNK activation, which is then relayed by short range signals including Upds and EGFs.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of ct inhibited the differentiation of injury-activated RSCs towards Alp4+ replacement PCs.

claim: Xanthine stones in Drosophila Malpighian tubules can be reproducibly generated by mutating the rosy (ry) gene, encoding xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH).

claim: In place of lost PCs, many new small cells appeared, some of which showed evidence of polyploidization.
